name: Team invitation
description: Invites someone into a workspace: who invited them, what they will be able to do, one action to accept, and the date the invitation stops working.

origin.note: Design: invitation card — the workspace set as the largest thing on the page, the inviter present as a quoted voice, one action and an expiry.

subject: {{ inviter_name }} invited you to join {{ workspace_name }}
preheader: One action to accept, and what the invitation lets you do once you are in.

credits.author: Jack Sparrow
credits.title: Man having an online meeting in an office

eyebrow.description: Small label above the workspace name. It does the work of a subject line for anyone who reads the email before the header.

workspace_name.description: The workspace, team or organisation being joined, set as the largest thing on the page. People accept an invitation to a place they recognise, so this is the name they know it by rather than an account slug.

inviter_name.description: Who is inviting them, by name. An invitation from a person converts; an invitation from a product does not, which is why the name leads the subject line as well.

role_name.description: The role they are being given, in the product's own vocabulary and without an article — the sentence supplies its own. It sets the expectation that the permissions list then keeps.

message.description: The inviter's own note, shown as a quotation in their voice. Optional, and worth prompting for in the product — a sentence of context is the difference between an invitation and a system message.
message.example: We are moving the September campaign in here this week, so you will want to be in before Thursday.

inviter_role.description: The inviter's job or role, shown under their name on the quotation. It answers the recipient's first question, which is whether this person can actually grant access.

inviter_avatar.description: Square photograph of the inviter, shown at 36px beside their name. Use a real photograph of the real person or leave it empty — a generated monogram in an email is a small lie that the reader can spot.

capabilities_heading.default: What you will be able to do

capabilities.description: What the role actually permits, as `text` and optional `detail`. Concrete abilities, and the notable limits too — someone who accepts expecting more than they get is a support ticket on their first day.

accept_label.description: Label for the one action this email exists for. Name the outcome — 'Accept and join Northwind' beats 'Continue'.

accept_url.description: The single-use acceptance link. This email carries one action and no competing links, because a second button measurably costs acceptances.

expires_at.description: When the link stops working, stated as a date rather than a countdown so it is still true when the email is read a week later. An invitation with no expiry is a credential with no expiry.

ignore_text.description: What to do if the invitation was unexpected. Saying that nothing happens until they accept is what makes it safe to ignore, and what makes the email look unlike a phishing attempt.
ignore_text.default: If you were not expecting this, you can ignore it. Nothing is created in your name until you accept, and the link stops working on its own.

sender_label.description: Lead-in for the sender address line.

inviter_email.description: The inviter's address, printed in full so the recipient can check it against someone they already correspond with before clicking anything.
